title: The Battlefront to Save Tamil
translation_notes: Fresh T1 translation made directly from the pinned Tamil after a complete P0/source review. No pre-existing English translation was consulted.
The repeated Tamil chapter heading at the start of the first extraction unit is represented only in title metadata, not duplicated as body prose.
The page-47/page-48 sentence split after 'எனக்குத்' and the page-48/page-49 personal-name split 'திரு என்.' / 'வி. நடராசன்' are reconstructed as continuous literary units.

paragraphs: Called by Tamils the "Fearless Heart," Pattukkottai Alagirisami arrayed a Tamil force at Tiruchirappalli and set out toward Madras. Among the prominent figures in that march were the venerable Moovalur Ramamirtham Ammaiyar and Manavai Thirumalaisami.

Alagirisami was a whirlwind orator of the Self-Respect Movement. Wanting nothing for himself, he devoted himself all day long to service to the country. The force and precision of the arguments heard in Periyar's speeches, the lines that bubbled with valour in Alagiri's speeches, and the beautiful Tamil of Anna's speeches greatly attracted me.

Alagiri was known as Summer-Thunder Alagiri. A broad, sturdy figure. A gait like a king whose head would never bow. A simple life. The news that a Tamil force under his leadership was coming toward Madras was, in those days, revolutionary indeed!

Moovalur Ammaiyar devoted herself to social service and carried out many good works in practical form. She conducted many widow remarriages and put the ideals of the Self-Respect Movement into practice. She took charge of preparing food and other necessities for the Tamil force all along its route.

Manavai Thirumalaisami was the editor of the weekly Nagarathoothan, writing political ideas in clipped, cutting strokes. When he wrote under the heading "Pen Dance," his pen truly danced! He too served as a commander of the Tamil force.

All along the two hundred miles from Tiruchirappalli to Madras, anti-Hindi supporters welcomed the Tamil force. Congress friends who supported Hindi caused it many troubles. They attacked with sticks. They hurled stones. Unshaken by anything, the Tamil force grew larger from town to town and marched heroically toward Madras.

On a village road, Congress men tied shoes into festoons and tried to humiliate the Tamil force by presenting them as a welcome. When people in that village who had Tamil feeling moved to untie and throw away those festoons, Alagirisami stopped them. He stood before the festoon and began to speak. People gathered in their thousands. Alagirisami did not stop. He went on speaking.
The tiger roared! The lion thundered! Summer thunder rumbled! Alagiri's speech went on for more than two hours.

"We are going to wipe away the stain that is about to fall upon Tamil and the Tamil. Is this the welcome you Tamils give us? If only you had spread on the ground the shoes you have hung in the sky, each of us could at least put on a pair and walk!" he thundered.

The flood of people roared and surged forward to cut down the festoon. Alagiri stopped them. "Let those who tied it untie it!" he said. Before his long speech had ended, the Congress men ran up to Alagiri, asked his forgiveness, and themselves untied and threw away the festoon they had put up. Not only that: they gave the Tamil force a tea reception and then sent it on its way.

All along that two-hundred-mile stretch, the Tamil force sowed anti-Hindi feeling in even the tiniest villages. I myself stood as an example of how the anti-Hindi cause drew students. Even in my school days I had a special interest in bringing many students together and forming associations—the Children's Reform Association, the Youth Association, and many more! Meetings every week! Speeches on special subjects!

In 1938, every evening I would line up many students and lead a procession through the streets of Tiruvarur. A Tamil flag in my hand! A cart bearing a picture of Rajaji trying to stab Tamil Mother with the dagger called compulsory Hindi! The procession under my leadership! A song I had written; all the students would raise it together:

"Come, all of us, let us go to war!
Let us drive back the Hindi demon that has come!"
That was the refrain of the song.

At that time, a man named Jagadeesan was on a hunger strike in Madras against Hindi. The fast stretched beyond sixty, seventy days. Periyar went to see him. It is said that the fasting man told Periyar of his desire for Periyar's green-stone ring. That very day, Periyar announced at a meeting that he had no faith in hunger strikes and such things.
In our student procession, we smashed to pieces the picture of that fasting man which I had been carrying in my hand every day. By then, he had already ended his fast.

One day, my class Hindi teacher saw our procession. I handed him the leaflet in my hand, filled with anti-Hindi slogans. He took it and went away without a word. The answer to it was waiting in class the next day.

Neither when I handed the leaflet to the Hindi teacher nor when I stood before him holding the Tamil flag and shouting, "Down with Hindi! Long live Tamil!" did I feel the slightest fear. In my bloodstream and in my breath, the feeling "Tamil! Tamil!" kept surging. Some may call that feeling frenzy. If attachment is to be called frenzy, then that meaning is perfectly right!

If one wants the finest proof that love of one's mother tongue rises above everything, it is this: Mr N. V. Natarajan, who had been working for the Congress Party in Madras's Peddunaickenpet, joined the movement to protect Tamil against the imposition of Hindi. Was it not because of the abundance of their love for Tamil that great Tamil scholars such as Maraimalai Adigal—who stood in the opposing camp on the ideas of the Self-Respect Movement—joined Self-Respect leader Periyar in opposing Hindi?

I was at an age, and possessed of a fervour, in which every throb of my beating heart sounded a Tamil melody. I considered even placing an anti-Hindi handbill in the Hindi teacher's hand to be a revolutionary act.
He wrote a few Hindi words on the blackboard in the classroom and ordered me to pronounce them. I stood up.
"Hm! Let's see you read them?" he said.
How could I read when I did not understand them? So I stood silent. He came near. The classroom seemed to be waiting eagerly for something. The teacher twisted my ear.
"Can you read or can't you?" he growled.
"I don't understand," I said.
He struck me hard across the cheek. My head spun as though the classroom itself were turning. I steadied myself and sat down on the wooden plank. I understood why the teacher had hit me.
"What I did during yesterday's procession was right! What he has done now is right too." Thus my heart rendered justice to me.

All the teachers expected that I would gather the students and launch some agitation, perhaps a strike, against the Hindi teacher! My brain did not work that way. The Hindi teacher himself stayed away from the high school for two or three days. At the gates of Tiruvarur High School too, activists of the Tamil movement carried on daily picketing as a righteous struggle. I stopped going to Hindi classes.
Thirty-six years have passed since that Hindi teacher struck me. About five years ago, that same Hindi teacher was waiting outside to take me to a homeopathy conference held in Mylapore, Madras.
Now he is no Hindi teacher! He is the head of a large institution that has trained many homeopathic doctors in Tamil Nadu.

When I think that I am one who sprouted from the language struggle that flared up in Tamil Nadu thirty-six years ago, without my knowing it a stately stride and a proud gaze come to me from somewhere!
It was in that very battlefront to save Tamil that the two Tamil bulls Thalamuthu and Natarajan became corpses in prison.

Speaking of compulsory Hindi, Anna said: "Compulsory Hindi became a good opportunity for our sense of race to well up, for our sacrifice to become known, for truth to come out, and for our labour to bear fruit. Our struggle has shown how many mothers are ready to go to prison for Tamil. It helped the light of gems like Thalamuthu and Natarajan—who would give even their lives—to be seen."

While the language war was going on in Tamil Nadu, Hindu-Muslim riots began to spread in the northern regions. Subhas Chandra Bose, touring East Bengal, had to face the opposition of Muslim people. Muhammad Ali Jinnah, on behalf of the Muslim League, threw down a challenge to the Congress Party. Gandhi described it as a "declaration of war."

The Muslim League pointed to the injustices inflicted on Muslims and the hardships they suffered in Congress-ruled provinces. The All-India Muslim League raised its voice condemning the compulsory Hindi imposed in Tamil Nadu's schools. In connection with this, Muslim League leaders in Tamil Nadu too marched in the ranks of the anti-Hindi opponents. Anti-Hindi conferences were held with the Tamil flag and the green crescent flag flying together.
